Proprotein Convertase Subtilisin/Kexin Type 9 (PCSK9)
Inhibitors for Treatment of High Cholesterol Levels
Effectiveness and Value
Jeffrey A. Tice, MD; Dhruv S. Kazi, MD, MSc, MS; Steven D. Pearson, MD, MSc
Source of Review
The Institute for Clinical and Economic Review developed an evi-
dencereport,includingasystematicreviewoftheliterature,acost-
effectiveness model, and a budget impact assessment, to support
a public meeting of the New
EnglandComparativeEffective-
ness Public Advisory Council
(CEPAC) on October 27, 2015.1
The report evaluates the comparative clinical effectiveness and
comparative value of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9
(PCSK9) inhibitors as a class for the treatment of adults with famil-
ial hypercholesterolemia or cardiovascular disease (CVD) who
require additional lowering of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol
(LDL-C) levels.
Background
Cardiovascular disease is the most common cause of death in the
United States.2 Aggressive reduction of LDL-C level with statin
therapymarkedlyreducedthenumbersofCVDevents.InJuly2015,
the US Food and Drug Administration FDA approved 2 monoclonal
antibodiestoPCSK9(alirocumabandevolocumab)thatlowerLDL-C
levels. The drugs are injected subcutaneously every 2 to 4 weeks.
The wholesale acquisition cost of these drugs ranges between
$14 100and$14 600peryear.Payersmustnowdecidehowtopro-
vide these drugs to their populations.
Summary of Findings
Twenty-five randomized trials including 10 159 patients compared
PCSK9 inhibitors with placebo and/or ezetimibe therapy for LDL-C
level lowering. Differences between alirocumab and evolocumab
wereminimal.ThepercentagereductioninLDL-ClevelswithPCSK9
inhibitor therapy was 59% greater than with placebo.3 There were
no significant increases in serious adverse events, neurocognitive
events,musclesymptoms,orliverenzymeelevations.Althoughcar-
diovascular events were not primary outcomes for any trials, com-
bined study results showed that there was a 50% reduction in the
odds of death from CVD (odds ratio [OR], 0.50; 95% CI, 0.23-1.10)
and myocardial infarction (OR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.26-0.93).3 How-
ever, there was a nonsignificant doubling in the odds of stroke (OR,
1.97;95%CI,0.69-5.65).Thesefindingsshouldbeinterpretedcau-
tiously because they reflect combined results from studies of 2 dif-
ferent drugs, different dosing schedules, different patient popula-
tions, and different comparison groups (placebo, ezetimibe).
While FDA approval was based on lowering LDL-C levels as an
acceptedsurrogateforimprovedcardiovascularoutcomes,thereare
countervailingexamplesfromtrialsofestrogentherapy,niacin,and
fibrates in which lowering LDL-C level did not improve CVD out-
comes. Torcetrapib offers a particularly sobering example: in a
15 000-person long-term randomized trial, torcetrapib lowered
LDL-C levels by 25% and raised high-density lipoprotein choles-
terol levels but also increased cardiovascular events by 25% and
increased total mortality by 58%.
Estimates of LDL-C level lowering were the key inputs for a
cost-effectiveness analysis using the CVD Policy Model, a vali-
dated model of coronary heart disease and stroke in the US popu-
lation older than 35 years.4 The model estimates the benefits and
costs for individuals in 3 high-risk populations: (1) those with
familial hypercholesterolemia (n = 605 000); (2) those with a
history of CVD and statin intolerance (n = 1 460 000); and
(3) those with history of CVD who require further LDL-C level low-
ering (based on having an LDL-C level 70 mg/dL while on a
statin therapy regimen) (n = 7 271 000). The primary outcome
was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for a PCSK9 inhibitor
compared with statin therapy based on population estimates
from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.
We used a health system perspective and a lifetime analytic
horizon.
For the population of individuals with familial hypercholester-
olemia, the model estimated that the number needed to treat for
5 years (NNT5) with a PCSK9 inhibitor to prevent 1 major adverse
cardiac event was 28. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio at
current prices was $290 000 per quality-adjusted life-year
(QALY) gained. Similarly, among patients with a history of CVD and
statin intolerance, the NNT5 for PCSK9 inhibitors was 21, with the
cost-effectiveness estimated at $274 000 per QALY gained.
Finally, among patients with a history of CVD whose LDL-C level
greater than 70 mg/dL, the NNT5 for PCSK9 inhibitors was also 21,
and the cost-effectiveness was $302 000 per QALY gained.
To evaluate whether the cost of a new drug is high enough to
warrant special efforts to constrain use in the short term, we esti-
matethepotentialbudgeteffectofnewdrugswithoutspecificpayer
or pharmacy benefit management controls in place. Assuming that
25% of all patients covered by the current FDA indications would
beprescribedPCSK9inhibitors(n = 2.6million)bytheendof5years,
the 5-year budget impact would be $107 billion nationwide.
The Figure presents results from 3 scenarios varying possible
drug prices, drug uptake patterns, and their effect on cost-
effectiveness ratios and the potential effect on budget. We evalu-
atedthedrugcostsatwhichPCSK9inhibitorswouldbeconsidered
cost-effectiveunderconventionalwillingness-to-paythresholdsof
$50 000/QALY, $100 000/QALY, and $150 000/QALY. The price
would need to be reduced to $3166, $5404, and $7735, respec-
tively, to meet these thresholds. These prices represent discounts
of42%to78%fromthewholesaleacquisitioncostofPCSK9inhibi-

tors. We also calculated the price at which the 5-year budget im-
pact would not exceed a growth target suggested by state and
national legislation of future gross domestic product plus 1%.5 The
resulting drug price of $2177 per year represented an 85%
discount from the average list price of these drugs ($14 350).
Limitations of the Evidence
The trials are limited by surrogate markers as the primary out-
comes. There is a lack of data from long-term studies with cardio-
vascular events as the primary outcome. Two 5-year trials random-
izingmorethan40 000participantsarescheduledtobecompleted
in 2017.6,7
Policy Discussions
TheCEPACvotedthatthePCSK9inhibitorshadlowvalue,basedon
thepoorlong-termcost-effectivenessandconcernsregardingshort-
term affordability. Key recommendations emerged from a multi-
stakeholder policy roundtable: (1) specialty societies should up-
date clinical guidance, including treatment goals based on target
LDL-C levels; (2) payers and providers should enhance health sys-
tem value by limiting treatment to patients for whom trials of high-
intensitystatinscombinedwithezetimibehavefailed;(3)clearclini-
calprotocolsneededtoidentifypatientswithtruestatinintolerance;
(4)restrictprescribingofPCSK9inhibitorstospecialistsinlipidman-
agement, given the complexities of caring for patients with familial
hypercholesterolemia or statin intolerance; and (5) should pricing
forPCSK9inhibitorsfall50%to85%relativetocurrentprices,much
of the proposed coverage policy requirements could be lifted.
Conclusions
The current evidence provides high certainty that PCSK9 inhibi-
tors lead to superior reductions in LDL-C levels compared with pla-
cebo and ezetimibe. Extrapolating from the LDL-C level reduc-
tions, our cost-effectiveness analysis estimates an NNT5 of 28.
These results assume clinical benefits that are being tested in
ongoing trials. Despite our favorable assumptions, cost-
effectiveness ratios for PCSK9 inhibitors far exceed commonly
accepted thresholds.8 Achieving cost-effectiveness at a threshold
of $100 000/QALY would require price reductions of 60% to
63% compared with current prices. Finally, our analysis suggests
that even deeper price reductions would be required to limit the
cost burden to the US health care system.
